passages.title: Passage 1
passages.instructions:
Questions 1–40

You should spend about 60 minutes on Questions 1–40, which are based on the reading passage below.
passages.body:
Social Media and Political Polarization

A Social media platforms enable rapid dissemination of political information, memes, and mobilisation appeals at scale, restructuring how citizens encounter news. Algorithmic feeds prioritise engagement, sometimes amplifying emotive or divisive content over nuanced policy analysis. Scholars debate whether digital environments cause polarization or reveal entrenched divisions accelerated by geographic sorting and partisan cable television precedents. Cross-national surveys find heterogeneous effects: some democracies report heightened affective hostility between party supporters, while others show stable attitudes despite increased online time spent arguing in comment threads. Scholars caution that cross-national comparisons require careful attention to institutional context and data quality.

B Echo chambers form when users follow ideologically similar accounts, reducing exposure to counterarguments unless platforms intentionally inject diverse sources. Experiments lowering algorithmic sorting modestly increase cross-cutting content yet rarely change deep beliefs measured weeks later. Bot networks and coordinated inauthentic behaviour manipulate trending topics, prompting platform integrity teams to label state-sponsored propaganda. Journalists rely on social listening tools to gauge sentiment, though sample bias toward vocal extremes can mislead campaign strategists about silent majorities less inclined to post publicly. Policy evaluations therefore depend on transparent reporting and independent replication of key results. Longitudinal studies remain essential before drawing firm conclusions about causal mechanisms and durable outcomes.

C Affective polarization emphasises tribal dislike more than policy disagreement, measured by feelings thermometer scores toward opposing partisans. Outrage cascades reward performative condemnation, training audiences to interpret compromise as betrayal. Politicians adapt by broadcasting clips optimized for sharing rather than legislative detail, shortening policy attention spans in legislatures already strained by omnibus bargaining. Civic educators promote media literacy curricula teaching lateral reading and source triangulation, yet funding fluctuates with political winds suspicious of critical thinking framed as ideological indoctrination by activist school boards. Longitudinal studies remain essential before drawing firm conclusions about causal mechanisms and durable outcomes.

D Regulatory proposals include transparency mandates on ad targeting, data portability, and duty-of-care duties for minors' mental health, contested by firms citing free expression. European digital services acts impose risk assessments for systemic platforms, while other jurisdictions experiment with age verification and default chronological feeds. Critics warn heavy-handed bans may push discourse into encrypted channels less visible to researchers monitoring extremist recruitment. The author argues regulation should distinguish amplification mechanisms from lawful speech, focusing on recommender accountability rather than policing every controversial opinion voiced by citizens in democratic debate. Scholars caution that cross-national comparisons require careful attention to institutional context and data quality.

E Offline consequences include harassment campaigns doxxing activists, threats against election workers, and street protests organised via event pages that outpace traditional party mobilisation structures. Police monitor live streams during demonstrations, blurring boundaries between public safety and surveillance. Some governments shut down networks during unrest, citing misinformation risks while suppressing dissent. Human rights advocates document gendered abuse deterring women from political speech online, perpetuating representation gaps in councils and parliaments despite hashtags celebrating visibility campaigns that rarely translate into safer participation without enforcement of platform harassment policies. Policy evaluations therefore depend on transparent reporting and independent replication of key results.

F Research methods leverage browser tracking, survey panels linked to digital traces, and field experiments randomising feed interventions with ethical oversight. Replication crises remind scholars that modest effects can be fragile across contexts. Longitudinal cohorts following adolescents into adulthood may clarify developmental impacts on civic trust, though causal inference remains contested when family background correlates with both platform use and political identity. Interdisciplinary teams combining computer science and sociology improve measurement of network structures beyond self-reported usage frequency alone, which poorly maps to actual exposure diversity. Longitudinal studies remain essential before drawing firm conclusions about causal mechanisms and durable outcomes.

G Looking ahead, the author believes healthier public spheres require platform design aligned with democratic values, not only shareholder metrics. Supporting local news and offline deliberative forums can counterbalance viral outrage economies. If technologists treat polarization solely as user pathology, institutional incentives creating engagement-maximising rage will persist. Shared standards for auditability, researcher data access, and user control over ranking algorithms offer a pragmatic path that preserves speech while reducing manipulative amplification that frays social cohesion necessary for collective problem solving on climate, health, and inequality. Scholars caution that cross-national comparisons require careful attention to institutional context and data quality.
